Getting started

Source: vignettes/matchdb.Rmd
matchdb.Rmd

You have a list of organizations: grant recipients, survey respondents, a contractor list. Each has a name and an address but no EIN. matchdb supplies the other side of the match: every name and address the IRS and 990 filers have recorded for each EIN. npmatch does the matching.

This walk-through matches four grant recipients, reads the results, and looks more closely at the ones that are not clear-cut. The output shown is from the published references of 2026-10-23.

1. Install 

remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/npmatch")
remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/matchdb")
library(matchdb)

2. Get a reference

A reference is the frame npmatch matches against. Four are published:

label which organizations which names rows
active-legal in the current BMF legal name and DBA 2.75M
active-observed in the current BMF legal, DBA, and names 2+ grantmakers wrote 2.89M
unified-legal in any BMF release legal name and DBA 4.98M
unified-observed in any BMF release legal, DBA, and names 2+ grantmakers wrote 5.14M

For current records, start with active-observed. The names grantmakers write (“American Red Cross”) are often not the legal name (“American National Red Cross”), and the observed names cover that gap. vignette("layers") explains when to use the unified-* tiers.

b <- md_reference("active-observed", fetch = "missing")

The first call downloads about 260 MB from the public NCCS copy; no AWS account is needed. Later calls read the local copy. Every file is checked against the md5 it was published with, and the bundle is refused if it was built by a different npmatch normalizer than the one installed. b holds:

  • reference: the frame;
  • name_freq and token_idf: corpus statistics, which tell npmatch how common a name or word is;
  • ref_index: the blocking index;
  • clusters: the families its organizations belong to.

3. Describe your records and match

np_query() maps your columns onto npmatch’s fields:

grants <- data.frame(
  id     = c("g1", "g2", "g3", "g4"),
  name   = c("American Red Cross", "Habitat for Humanity of Greater Boston",
             "Boys & Girls Club of Dane County", "Friends of the Ellsworth Public Library"),
  street = c("431 18th Street NW", "434 Massachusetts Ave Suite 201",
             "5215 Verona Road", "20 State Street"),
  city   = c("Washington", "Boston", "Fitchburg", "Ellsworth"),
  state  = c("DC", "MA", "WI", "ME"),
  zip    = c("20006", "02118", "53711", "04605"))

q <- npmatch::np_query(grants, c(.id = "id", name = "name", street = "street",
                                 city = "city", state = "state", zip5 = "zip"))

m <- npmatch::np_cascade(q, b$reference,
                         name_freq = b$name_freq, token_idf = b$token_idf,
                         ref_index = b$ref_index)

4. Read the results

Each query gets a tier: YES (accept), MAYBE (a good candidate that needs a look) or NO. It also gets the best EIN found and the reference name that won.

as.data.frame(m)[, c(".id", "tier", "overall_ein", "overall_name_y", "overall_score")]
#>   .id  tier    overall_ein                          overall_name_y overall_score
#> 1  g1 MAYBE EIN-53-0196605                      AMERICAN RED CROSS         0.680
#> 2  g4 MAYBE EIN-01-0498465 FRIENDS OF THE ELLSWORTH PUBLIC LIBRARY         0.980
#> 3  g3 MAYBE EIN-39-1925617  BOYS AND GIRLS CLUB OF DANE COUNTY INC         0.980
#> 4  g2   YES EIN-04-2994233 HABITAT FOR HUMANITY GREATER BOSTON INC         0.927

All four found the right organization. Only one is a YES, and each MAYBE is a MAYBE for a different reason.

  • g2, Habitat for Humanity: YES. Name and address agree, and nothing else comes close.
  • g1, American Red Cross: MAYBE. The name matched exactly, on an observed name: grantmakers write AMERICAN RED CROSS, and active-observed carries that spelling. But each observed name comes paired with the address grantmakers wrote next to it, usually a local chapter, not headquarters. Name and address therefore point at different rows (views_agree is FALSE), and npmatch holds it at MAYBE.
  • g4, Friends of the Ellsworth Public Library: MAYBE. Exact name and address, but LIBRARY triggers npmatch’s soft government_entity veto, since many libraries are government units without an EIN of their own. Here the friends group is a nonprofit, and a reviewer would accept it.
  • g3, Boys & Girls Club of Dane County: MAYBE, tie. Three EINs scored 0.98. That is a family, not a mistake, as the next section shows.

The full result has the reasons in columns: pass, runner_up_score, tie, n_close, overall_veto_reason, views_agree, name_ein and addr_ein.

5. Look closer

With the database downloaded, md_lookup() shows everything known about an EIN, and md_cluster() shows its families. The database is about 10 GB, and md_fetch_db() downloads it once.

md_fetch_db()
md_cluster("39-1925617", types = c("related_system", "shared_website"))
#> <md_cluster> EIN-39-1925617: 4 clusters (related_system 3, shared_website 1)
#>
#>   SYS-87-4664285  related_system, 2 members  BOYS & GIRLS CLUB OF DANE COUNTY FOUNDATION INC
#>       EIN-87-4664285  BOYS & GIRLS CLUB OF DANE COUNTY FOUNDAT WI
#>     * EIN-39-1925617  BOYS AND GIRLS CLUB OF DANE COUNTY INC WI
#>
#>   WEB-bgcdc.org  shared_website, 3 members
#>     * EIN-39-1925617  BOYS AND GIRLS CLUB OF DANE COUNTY INC WI
#>       EIN-87-4618323  BOYS & GIRLS CLUB OF DANE COUNTY LEGACY  WI
#>       EIN-87-4664285  BOYS & GIRLS CLUB OF DANE COUNTY FOUNDAT WI
#>   ...

The club, its foundation and its legacy fund share a website, two addresses and a Schedule R relationship. The tie in g3 is between them. Whether a grant “to the Boys & Girls Club” belongs to the club or its foundation is a judgement the data can only flag. The club, the operating entity, is the usual answer.

x <- md_lookup("53-0196605")
x
#> <md_lookup> EIN-53-0196605  AMERICAN NATIONAL RED CROSS
#>   layer bmf_active, active TRUE, NTEE P210, subsection 3
#>   names      1800 rows (dba 1, in_care_of 1, legal 2, observed 1796)
#>   addresses  2863 rows
#>   ...
head(x$names[x$names$variant_class == "observed", c("name_raw", "n_corroborators")])
#>                                   name_raw n_corroborators
#> 4                       AMERICAN RED CROSS            1292
#> 5              AMERICAN NATIONAL RED CROSS             377
#> 6                                RED CROSS              40
#> 7 AMERICAN RED CROSS NATIONAL HEADQUARTERS              35
#> 8                   THE AMERICAN RED CROSS              24
#> 9            AMERICAN RED CROSS - NATIONAL              19

1,292 different grantmakers wrote AMERICAN RED CROSS for this EIN. That is why active-observed carries the spelling, and why g1 found the right organization even though the name is not the legal one.

6. Match one level up

Two npmatch functions read those families alongside the scored candidates.

np_pair_links() reports whether each query’s top two candidates are one family:

npmatch::np_pair_links(m, b$clusters)[, c(".id", "top_ein", "runner_up_ein", "linked", "link_types")]
#>   .id        top_ein  runner_up_ein linked                              link_types
#> 1  g1 EIN-53-0196605 EIN-52-0743599   TRUE                               co_tenant
#> 2  g2 EIN-04-2994233 EIN-04-3348433   TRUE                   brand;group_exemption
#> 3  g3 EIN-39-1925617 EIN-87-4664285   TRUE co_tenant;related_system;shared_website
#> 4  g4 EIN-01-0498465 EIN-47-5330473  FALSE

A tie between linked EINs (g3) is a family to settle. A tie between strangers is a real ambiguity.

np_cluster_rollup() handles split evidence: the name matches one member of a family and the address another, so no single EIN scores well but the family does. It returns nothing for these four, because each found its organization directly. On 1,984 Schedule I records with a known EIN, it placed 60 of 739 non-YES records in a family, and the true EIN was in that family 90% of the time.

npmatch::np_cluster_rollup(m, b$clusters, query = npmatch::np_normalize(q))

7. Build your own reference

The published tiers cover the common cases. For anything else, describe the slice with md_spec() and compile it from the database:

s <- md_spec(layers = c("bmf_active", "bmf_inactive", "postcard_only"),
             names = c("legal", "dba", "observed"),
             addresses = c("mailing", "observed"),
             min_corroborators = 2,
             label = "everything-small-orgs-too")
r <- md_compile(s)
#> spec 5f3050225dde786f: 5,211,807 rows over 3,771,700 EINs
r$report          # rows by class, rows per EIN, family members left out

m2 <- npmatch::np_cascade(q, r$reference, name_freq = r$name_freq,
                          token_idf = r$token_idf,
                          ref_index = npmatch::np_ref_index(r$reference))

A spec has a hash, so the same spec always gives the same reference on any machine. To keep a slice, md_publish(s) writes it as a stamped bundle, and md_reference("everything-small-orgs-too") reads it back.
